title: Synapses in the Brain: Adhesion, Scaffolds and Astrocytes

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Which measurements establish that a synaptic contact is anatomically present?
cards.back: Electron microscopy, or staining that shows presynaptic and postsynaptic proteins side by side.
cards.quote: You see it by electron microscopy, or by staining for presynaptic and postsynaptic proteins that sit side by side.
cards.section: Three things a working synapse does

cards.front: Why should vesicle recycling and postsynaptic currents be measured separately when evaluating a developing synapse?
cards.back: Recycling measures vesicle release and retrieval; postsynaptic currents measure receptor responses. A terminal can release transmitter without producing a particular receptor response.
cards.quote: A synapse can respond through one kind of receptor and not another.
cards.section: Three things a working synapse does

cards.front: A factor is {{c1::necessary}} for an effect if the effect does not happen without it.
cards.quote: It is necessary if the effect does not happen without it.
cards.section: Three things a working synapse does

cards.front: Why does adding a protein to a permissive culture test a different claim from deleting its gene in an animal?
cards.back: Adding it tests sufficiency under those conditions; deletion tests necessity. Producing an effect when added does not establish that the effect requires it.
cards.quote: A factor is sufficient if adding it is enough to produce an effect in a system that is otherwise ready, under the conditions tested.
cards.section: Three things a working synapse does

cards.front: How does the input pattern of a typical brain neuron differ from that of a mature mammalian muscle fiber?
cards.back: A brain neuron receives thousands of inputs using multiple transmitters. A mature muscle fiber usually receives one motor axon at one site, using acetylcholine.
cards.quote: Excitatory synapses that use glutamate and inhibitory synapses that use GABA sit on the same dendrite.
cards.section: Why central synapses are harder than the neuromuscular junction

cards.front: A hypothetical signal clusters receptors at new cortical contacts but cannot distinguish glutamatergic from GABAergic inputs. Would it alone ensure correctly specified synapses, and why?
cards.back: No. Each contact also needs the appropriate receptor type; receptor clustering alone cannot specify whether a contact will be excitatory or inhibitory.
cards.quote: Each contact has to specify what kind of synapse it will be.
cards.section: Why central synapses are harder than the neuromuscular junction

cards.front: Why can an isolated axon or dendrite show synaptic specializations without having a stable synapse?
cards.back: Both sides assemble some components before meeting. Contact enlarges and stabilizes those initial specializations to form a lasting synapse.
cards.quote: Each side can form its specialization alone, but stable synapses require both: contact enlarges and stabilizes what each side began.
cards.section: Why central synapses are harder than the neuromuscular junction

cards.front: Synaptic adhesion signals that instruct a partner to build its side of a synapse are called {{c1::organizers}}.
cards.quote: acting as organizers: signals that tell a partner to build its side of a synapse.
cards.section: Signals that turn a growth cone into a nerve terminal

cards.front: At the cerebellar mossy fiber–granule cell synapse, which side carries neurexin and which carries neuroligin?
cards.back: Neurexin is on the axon; neuroligin is on the granule cell dendrite.
cards.quote: Neurexins are axon-side membrane proteins; neuroligins, made by granule cells, are their dendrite-side partners.
cards.section: Signals that turn a growth cone into a nerve terminal

cards.front: Depolarized axons contacting neuroligin-expressing kidney cells take up antibodies to the normally internal face of synaptotagmin. What does uptake establish beyond vesicle clustering?
cards.back: The vesicles release and are retrieved. The antibody can reach its target only when a vesicle opens to the outside, so the clusters support vesicle cycling.
cards.quote: which they can reach only when a vesicle opens to the outside. So vesicles were being released and retrieved there.
cards.section: Signals that turn a growth cone into a nerve terminal

cards.front: A proposed block of Wnt7a in developing cerebellar mossy fibers is claimed to prevent every terminal from forming. What outcome is supported by the loss-of-function evidence, and why?
cards.back: Delayed terminal maturation is supported; complete prevention is not established. Wnt7a promotes spreading, branching and synapsin I gathering, and its deletion delayed maturation.
cards.quote: In mice lacking Wnt7a, maturation of the mossy fiber terminals was delayed.
cards.section: Signals that turn a growth cone into a nerve terminal

cards.front: Which granule cell signal promotes mossy fiber vesicle clustering through a receptor tyrosine kinase, and which receptor does it use?
cards.back: FGF22 acts through FGFR2 on mossy fiber axons.
cards.quote: FGF22, made by granule cells, promotes vesicle clustering in mossy fiber axons through FGFR2, a receptor tyrosine kinase
cards.section: Signals that turn a growth cone into a nerve terminal

cards.front: {{c1::AMPA receptors}} are glutamate-gated channels that carry most fast excitatory current.
cards.quote: AMPA receptors are the glutamate-gated channels that carry most fast excitatory current
cards.section: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors

cards.front: Why can glutamate fail to produce much NMDA receptor current near rest even when a co-agonist is bound?
cards.back: Physiological extracellular magnesium blocks most NMDA current near rest. Depolarization relieves that block.
cards.quote: in physiological extracellular magnesium most of their current is blocked near the resting potential; depolarization relieves the block.
cards.section: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors

cards.front: Which partners bind the first two versus the third PDZ domains of PSD-95?
cards.back: The first two bind NMDA receptor GluN2 tails; the third binds the neuroligin tail.
cards.quote: The first two PDZ domains bind the tail of NMDA receptor GluN2 subunits. The third binds the tail of neuroligin.
cards.section: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors

cards.front: How does stargazin connect AMPA receptors to the postsynaptic scaffold in cerebellar granule cells?
cards.back: It binds AMPA receptors and brings them to the surface; its tail binds PSD-95 PDZ domains to hold them at synapses.
cards.quote: stargazin binds AMPA receptors and brings them to the cell surface, and that its tail, which binds PSD-95's PDZ domains, holds them at synapses.
cards.section: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors

cards.front: Design a comparison that tests whether stargazin’s PSD-95-binding tail is needed for synaptic anchoring rather than surface delivery in granule cells lacking stargazin.
cards.back: Compare full-length stargazin with a mutant lacking the PDZ-binding tail. Measure surface AMPA labeling and synaptic AMPA currents separately. Restored surface labeling without restored currents would support a distinct anchoring role.
cards.quote: its tail, which binds PSD-95's PDZ domains, holds them at synapses.
cards.section: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors

cards.front: Which scaffold holds glycine receptors and many GABA-A receptors at inhibitory synapses?
cards.back: Gephyrin.
cards.quote: Gephyrin forms dense clusters under the terminal that hold glycine receptors and many GABA-A receptors.
cards.section: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors

cards.front: A treatment increases mossy fiber synapse counts in stargazer granule cells but leaves AMPA currents absent. Has it repaired the known defect, and what must a successful rescue restore?
cards.back: No. A rescue must restore AMPA receptor delivery to the surface and retention at synapses, verified by surface labeling and synaptic AMPA currents. The rules are that stargazin supports both steps and anatomical presence does not establish receptor function.
cards.quote: What fails is one kind of response: the same synapse responds through NMDA receptors but not through AMPA receptors.
cards.section: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors

cards.front: Why can neuroligin induce a terminal in a dish while neuroligin 1–3 knockout mice still form normal numbers of brainstem synapses?
cards.back: Dish sufficiency does not imply necessity for formation in vivo. Other organizers may overlap; the knockout nevertheless impairs transmission, especially at inhibitory synapses.
cards.quote: One likely reason is that several organizers overlap, so removing one family leaves others to start contacts;
cards.section: A dish shows what a protein can do; a mouse shows what the brain needs

cards.front: Neuroligin 1–3 knockout brainstem synapses have normal counts but impaired transmission. Can those two measurements alone locate the defect to transmitter release or receptor response?
cards.back: No. They separate anatomical presence from transmission but do not separate release from response. Add a vesicle-cycling assay and receptor-specific postsynaptic recordings.
cards.quote: A signal can change more than one of the three properties, and each experiment sees only the ones it measures.
cards.section: Three things a working synapse does

cards.front: Two candidate organizers each induce terminals when expressed alone on non-neuronal cells, yet either single deletion leaves counts normal. How would you test whether they overlap in initiating contacts?
cards.back: Compare single and combined deletions, measuring both counts and transmission. A count deficit only after combined deletion would support overlap. This follows the rule that sufficiency does not establish necessity and the proposed overlap among organizers.
cards.quote: One likely reason is that several organizers overlap, so removing one family leaves others to start contacts;
cards.section: A dish shows what a protein can do; a mouse shows what the brain needs

cards.front: A {{c1::miniature current}} is the small synaptic current caused by one vesicle released on its own.
cards.quote: A miniature current, or mini, is the small current from one vesicle released on its own.
cards.section: Astrocytes: building and switching on

cards.front: Why block action potentials when comparing spontaneous miniature synaptic currents between neuron cultures?
cards.back: It removes release driven by firing, so differences do not simply reflect how often the neurons fire.
cards.quote: Tetrodotoxin blocks action potentials, which removes release driven by firing, so what remains depends on the synapses and not on how busy the neurons are.
cards.section: Astrocytes: building and switching on

cards.front: Purified neurons show more miniature currents after receiving astrocyte-conditioned medium. Survival is unchanged. What does this support about the glial influence, and what alternative is weakened?
cards.back: A released glial factor can influence synapses without direct contact. Unchanged survival weakens the explanation that the effect merely reflects more surviving neurons.
cards.quote: A layer of glia across the dish, not touching the neurons, or medium the glia had conditioned, changed the picture.
cards.section: Astrocytes: building and switching on

cards.front: In a hypothetical neuron culture, minis rise from 10 to 90 per minute and contact number triples. If the detectable fraction is unchanged and the rest reflects spontaneous release, how much does release rate per synapse rise?
cards.back: Total mini frequency rises 90/10 = 9-fold. Per-synapse release rises 9/3 = 3-fold, assuming the same fraction of contacts produces detectable minis.
cards.quote: detected mini frequency ≈ (synapses giving detectable minis) × (their average rate of releasing a vesicle on its own)
cards.section: Astrocytes: building and switching on

cards.front: After a culture treatment, contact counts are unchanged, detected minis become more frequent, and mini amplitudes increase. Does this establish increased spontaneous release per synapse?
cards.back: No. Larger events may cross the detection threshold, increasing the fraction of contacts giving detectable minis. Check detection with noise and recording conditions controlled before assigning the rise to release. The rule is that detected frequency depends on both detectable contacts and release rate.
cards.quote: The minis also got larger, so some extra events may simply have become big enough to detect.
cards.section: Astrocytes: building and switching on

cards.front: Why are thrombospondin-induced synapses in purified neuron cultures called postsynaptically silent near rest?
cards.back: They release transmitter but lack working AMPA responses; any NMDA receptors present would be mostly magnesium-blocked near rest.
cards.quote: Those synapses looked normal by electron microscopy and released transmitter but were postsynaptically silent: they give no AMPA response near rest.
cards.section: Astrocytes: building and switching on

cards.front: Glypicans 4 and 6 are added to thrombospondin-treated neuron cultures with releasing but AMPA-silent synapses. What functional change is expected, and why?
cards.back: AMPA responses should appear as receptors are recruited to synapses. This complements thrombospondin’s building effect; the assays do not establish a fixed order of action.
cards.quote: including glypicans 4 and 6, which recruit AMPA receptors and make such synapses respond,
cards.section: Astrocytes: building and switching on

cards.front: At 37 °C, use E(Cl) = 61 mV × log10([Cl]inside/[Cl]outside). With 30 mM inside and 130 mM outside, calculate E(Cl) and predict GABA-A’s voltage effect from −60 mV, neglecting bicarbonate.
cards.back: E(Cl) = 61 × log10(30/130) ≈ −39 mV. Opening chloride channels pulls voltage toward −39 mV, so it depolarizes from −60 mV.
cards.why: Chloride flows out because E(Cl) is above the membrane potential.
cards.quote: With 30 mM chloride inside and 130 mM outside, E(Cl) is about −39 mV,
cards.section: Maturation: GABA changes sign

cards.front: A neuron rests at −60 mV with E(Cl) at about −77 mV. Neglect bicarbonate. When GABA-A channels open, which way does chloride move, and what happens to voltage?
cards.back: Chloride enters and voltage moves toward −77 mV, hyperpolarizing the neuron.
cards.quote: With 7 mM inside, E(Cl) is about −77 mV, and the same channel now hyperpolarizes.
cards.section: Maturation: GABA changes sign

cards.front: Why does a depolarizing GABA-A response not necessarily increase neuronal firing?
cards.back: Open GABA-A channels can shunt current and damp firing even while depolarizing the membrane.
cards.quote: An open GABA-A channel also damps firing by shunting current,
cards.section: Maturation: GABA changes sign

cards.front: A developing rodent cortical neuron gains KCC2 while its GABA-A receptors remain present. Predict the change in GABA’s voltage effect and explain why a synapse count would miss it.
cards.back: As KCC2 lowers internal chloride enough to move E(Cl) below rest, GABA changes from depolarizing to hyperpolarizing. Counts miss the altered ionic driving force. This combines the chloride-gradient rule with the rule that anatomical presence does not describe functional response.
cards.quote: As KCC2 rises over the first postnatal weeks, internal chloride falls.
cards.section: Maturation: GABA changes sign

cards.front: A protein makes contacting axons accumulate vesicles in culture. Design the next steps to establish functional presynaptic differentiation there and test whether the animal requires it for normal synapses.
cards.back: Test stimulated vesicle recycling and compare equally contacted control cells. Delete the protein in the animal, then count synapses and record transmission. The rules are that clustering alone does not demonstrate release, and culture sufficiency does not establish necessity in the animal.
cards.quote: Then both count synapses, by electron microscopy or staining, and record transmission, with evoked and miniature currents.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Classical cadherins bind the same cadherin on a facing cell only when {{c1::calcium}} is present.
cards.quote: bind the same cadherin on the facing cell (homophilic binding) only when calcium is present.
cards.section: Adhesion proteins that span the cleft

cards.front: A receptor-rich membrane patch detects acetylcholine released from cultured frog or chick growth cones before muscle contact. Which claim about presynaptic development does this rule out?
cards.back: It rules out muscle contact being required for the first transmitter release in these cultures. It does not show that stable synapses form without partners.
cards.quote: growth cones of cultured frog and chick neurons release acetylcholine before reaching a muscle,
cards.section: Early growth-cone experiments and the calcium signal

cards.front: In mouse sympathetic ganglia deprived of target-derived NGF, preganglionic axons still arrive but postsynaptic assembly fails. What follows for presynaptic assembly, and why is axon arrival insufficient evidence of a synapse?
cards.back: Presynaptic assembly should also fail. In this system, NGF-dependent postsynaptic assembly is a prerequisite for presynaptic assembly. Axon arrival alone tests neither assembled receiving sites nor transmitter release; the rule separates reaching a target from building a functioning synapse.
cards.quote: postsynaptic assembly is in turn a prerequisite for presynaptic assembly, although preganglionic axons still grow into the ganglion without the growth factor.
cards.section: Target-derived NGF and postsynaptic assembly in sympathetic ganglia

cards.front: At one stimulus per second in the glial add-back cultures, evoked failure falls from about 1/5 to 1/50. Under the simple Poisson model, mean vesicles per stimulus = −ln(failure fraction). Estimate each mean and the fold change.
cards.back: Before: −ln(1/5) ≈ 1.6 vesicles per stimulus. After: −ln(1/50) ≈ 3.9. The ratio is about 2.4-fold. This assumes failure means zero vesicles released.
cards.quote: Under a simple Poisson model, in which a stimulus fails only when no vesicle is released,
cards.section: Three readouts in the glial add-back experiments

cards.front: Why should the twelvefold mini-frequency increase in the glial add-back cultures not be used as the fold increase in evoked vesicle output?
cards.back: They measure different release conditions. Detected minis depend on spontaneous release and detectability; evoked failures estimate release per stimulus under a separate model.
cards.quote: That is close to the 2.3-fold rise in synapse number in the same cultures and far from the twelvefold rise in minis.
cards.section: Three readouts in the glial add-back experiments

cards.front: Why is E(Cl) only an approximation to the GABA-A current reversal potential, and why does the mature example still hyperpolarize?
cards.back: GABA-A channels also pass bicarbonate, shifting reversal above E(Cl). In the mature example, reversal remains below rest, so opening the channels still hyperpolarizes.
cards.quote: GABA-A channels also pass bicarbonate, so the reversal potential of the GABA current sits a little above E(Cl).
cards.section: The reversal potential of the GABA current
